To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
penultimate primary word stress is more likely to occur in Dutch and English words with four than three syllables, and that this length effect is not present in German.
the location of primary (penultimate) stress in trisyllable and quadrisyllable words differs between Dutch and German on the one hand and English on the other.
the location of primary syllable stress in Dutch, English, and German is influenced by word length, and that the effect of word length is larger in English and German than in Dutch.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of phonological and morphological constraints on the location of primary lexical stress in three closely related Germanic languages.
the interaction of word length and stress location in the three languages, and with the extent to which this interaction can be described in terms of language-universal principles.

the extent to which language-specific constraints affect the distribution of stress in polysyllabic words, and it also addresses the question of how speakers' intuitions about stress assignment can be used in the study of the distribution of stress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the location of primary lexical stress in the three languages is affected by the number of syllables preceding the final three syllables.
the location of primary syllable stress in monomorphemic Dutch, German, or English words is not a function of the number of syllables preceding the final three syllables.

in the three languages studied, word length is a relevant factor in determining the location of primary lexical stress, but that this factor is not the only one, and that there are important intra- and inter-speaker variations in this respect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the length of a word affects the location of its primary stress, but that this effect is not as straightforward as one would expect on the basis of the phonological rules of the languages involved.
in all three language, the length effect is present but that it is more pronounced in English and German than in Dutch.
there is a strong preference for primary word stress on the final syllable of trisyllabic Dutch, German, English words.
The main takeaway from our work is that
word length is an important variable for understanding stress assignment in Dutch, German and English.
the syllabic structure of words is a crucial factor in the assignment of primary stress in all three languages.
the location of primary stressed syllables in monomorphemic Dutch, German, English words is influenced by the number of syllables preceding the final syllable.
